title: Personality, tastes and first impressions
subtitle: Je le trouve vraiment sympa !
summary: Describe someone's personality, say how much you like people and things, and react to gossip about colleagues.

lesson.heading: Talking about colleagues
lesson.text: Two colleagues gossip about the people they work with. To give your opinion of someone, use **je le / je la trouve** + adjective (I find him / her ...). **Il a l'air** + adjective means he *seems* or *looks* that way.

examples.note: Do you know Patrice well?

examples.text: *Émilie :* **Je le trouve** vraiment antipathique. **Il a l'air** faux.
examples.note: I find him really unpleasant. He seems two-faced.

examples.text: Elle est très sympa ! Elle est toujours **de bonne humeur**.
examples.note: She's very nice! She's always in a good mood.

examples.text: Il n'est pas beau, mais il **a beaucoup de charme**.
examples.note: He isn't good-looking, but he has a lot of charm.
He / she is a shy person.

lesson.heading: Key expressions
lesson.text: Short reactions you will hear in any conversation about other people.

examples.note: By chance.
I've no idea!
That's completely different! / That has nothing to do with it!
There's no need.
That's not nice!
Well, that's amazing! - surprise or indignation
She's seeing someone. / She's in a relationship.
After all, why not?

lesson.heading: How much do you like them?
lesson.text: With people, the verbs go up a scale. Surprisingly, **aimer** on its own is the *strongest*: it means love. Add **bien** for simple liking and **beaucoup** for friendship. With things, use the definite article: *j'aime **le** basket*.

examples.note: I like Lucien. (I find him nice)
I'm very fond of Lucien. (friendship)
I love Lucien. / I love you!
I don't like Joël. I hate Joël.

examples.text: J'aime bien le basket, j'**adore** le rugby, mais j'**ai horreur de** la natation !
examples.note: I like basketball, I love rugby, but I can't stand swimming!

lesson.heading: La personnalité - opposites
lesson.note: **Sympathique** (familiar: **sympa**) means nice; its opposite **antipathique** is a very strong word. *C'est quelqu'un de bien* = he / she is a good, decent person.

lesson.heading: Il est ... or il a l'air ...?

left.label: être + adjective
left.text: You know the person: it is a fact.

right.label: avoir l'air + adjective
right.text: Just an impression - he *looks* or *seems* it.

lesson.heading: How a relationship starts
lesson.text: To say someone attracts you, French turns the sentence round: **plaire à** means *to be liked by*, so *Virginie plaît à Boniface* = Boniface likes Virginie.

examples.note: Boniface meets Virginie at university.

examples.text: Virginie **plaît à** Boniface. Il **est attiré par** elle.
examples.note: Boniface likes Virginie. He is attracted to her.
He finds her pretty and nice.
Virginie has noticed Boniface.
She's starting to take an interest in Boniface.

lesson.text: The French prize the art of conversation: speaking clearly and brilliantly counts for a lot. Edmond Rostand's hero Cyrano de Bergerac (1897) is ugly but wins hearts with words - and the French, alas, also have a reputation for arrogance!

exercises.prompt: Match each quality with its opposite.

context.label: From the dialogue
context.text:
*Adrienne :* Tu connais bien Patrice ?
*Émilie :* Oui, hélas, je le connais... Je le déteste ! Je le trouve vraiment antipathique.

exercises.explanation: She finds him **antipathique** - the opposite of *sympathique*. She even says *je le déteste*.

context.label: From the dialogue
context.text: *Clotilde :* Je la vois tous les jours. Je l'appelle souvent. Je l'ai invitée au cinéma, en boîte avec nos copains, à un pique-nique... Elle refuse toujours !

exercises.statement: Clotilde a invité Babette plusieurs fois.
exercises.explanation: She invited her to the cinema, a club and a picnic - several times.

context.label: From the dialogue
context.text:
*Philippe :* Vous avez le numéro de mobile de Patrice ?
*Jean-Paul :* Oui, je l'ai. Je l'ai noté sur un papier. Un instant... Ah, non, je ne le trouve plus !

exercises.statement: Jean-Paul donne le numéro de mobile de Patrice.
exercises.explanation: He wrote it down but **can't find it any more** (*je ne le trouve plus*), so he can't give it.

exercises.prompt: Match each line with the best reply.

pairs.right: Non, ça n'a rien à voir !

pairs.left: Il dit que tu ne le vois jamais !
pairs.right: Ça, c'est extraordinaire ! Je le rencontre tous les jours !

pairs.left: Comment est-ce qu'ils se sont rencontrés ?

pairs.right: Alors, pourquoi est-ce qu'il ne l'invite pas ?

pairs.left: Je peux le contacter, si tu veux.
pairs.right: Non, ce n'est pas la peine.

exercises.prompt: *« Vous savez si Colette est là ? »* Which reply makes sense?
exercises.explanation: The question asks *whether* she's there, so the answer is about knowing a fact: **je ne sais pas**.

exercises.prompt: Elle l'a rencontré par ___, chez des amis.
Est-ce qu'elle est généreuse ? — Non, au contraire, elle est ___.
exercises.explanation: The opposite of *généreux / généreuse* is **égoïste** (same form for both genders).

exercises.prompt: You are talking about a woman. Which sentences say you like her, and which say you can't stand her?

items.text: Elle est toujours de bonne humeur.

exercises.prompt: You have just met a man for the first time. He seems shy, but you don't really know him yet. What do you say?
exercises.explanation: **Avoir l'air** + adjective gives an impression; *il est timide* states a fact you are sure of.

exercises.prompt: Michel est mon grand amour : je l'___.
exercises.hint: aimer or détester? add bien or beaucoup only if needed
exercises.explanation: For love, use **aimer** on its own - *je l'aime*. *Aimer bien* would only mean you like him.

exercises.prompt: Build the sentence: "I find him really unpleasant."
exercises.explanation: **Trouver quelqu'un** + adjective; the pronoun *le* goes before the verb.
